title: Recording with Jimmy Smith
summary: Babs Gonzalez arranged the Jimmy Smith link and Donaldson praises Smith's blues feel and genius.

blocks.x: You did so many gigs with Jimmy Smith in 1957 and 1958. People still treasure those recordings and play them, they’re a firm part of the history. When did you start establishing a performing relationship with Jimmy Smith?
‘57, ‘58, somewhere in there...
Where I’m going is, was it set up by the record company? Was it your initiative?
No. Babs Gonzalez set that up. He brought Jimmy to New York and told Alfred he should record him. So Babs was in the middle of that.
So Jimmy Smith got the date, and then you got the call to do the record?
Yes.
Were those satisfying engagements?
Oh, yeah. No doubt about it. The Sermon is one of the greatest records ever made. It’s a great record.
What do you think was the key to your simpatico with Jimmy Smith?
We were compatible. He liked me. The organ sound and the alto sound is beautiful. Yeah, he liked me, because I played the blues, and that’s what he played.
Can you describe personally what he was like during those sessions?
Jimmy? Jimmy was carefree. Nice guy. In his latter years they said he was something else, but I didn’t know him then. I hadn’t seen him in a while. But back then, he was just a carefree guy.
Had you heard before he played organ, when he was a piano player?

No, I hadn’t heard him when he was piano player. The first I heard him was a record he made down in Wilmington. That’s where I heard that record, and it was so dynamic. With Thornell Schwartz. That was a great record.
Had you been playing with organ players before that?
Not too many. I played with John Patton.
Before Jimmy Smith?
Oh, yeah. I played with John Patton, Baby Face Willette, a couple of guys.
The records with John Patton are around 1960, with Baby Face Willette around 1961. I wanted you to tell us about the Jimmy Smith recordings just because the records are so great...
Yeah, they’re great.
So whatever insight you can give us into how they were set up, or how...
Jimmy was a musical genius. He can play. He was just like Art Tatum at the piano. It’s hard to play anything that he hasn’t played.
Did that give you a feeling of freedom, that you could...
Uh...yeah, freedom. Inspiration. Because he had good basslines. He could kick it.
